triples.relationship: wealth associated with deceit and impiety
triples.rationale: Micah links accumulated wealth with impiety and the inhabitants' false speech. Jeremiah likewise describes houses filled with deceit whose owners became great and rich, followed by their failure to judge rightly and the promise of visitation.
triples.source_text: From these they filled their wealth with impiety; those inhabiting her spoke falsehoods, and their tongue was exalted in their mouth.

target_units.text: For impious people were found among My people, and they set traps to destroy men and were catching them.
Like a set trap full of birds, so their houses are full of deceit; therefore they became great and rich.
And they transgressed judgment; they did not judge an orphan’s case, and they were not judging a widow’s case.
Shall I not visit for these things? says the Lord. Or will not My soul take vengeance on such a nation?

triples.relationship: punishment for sins preceding agricultural deprivation
triples.rationale: Micah announces striking and obliteration because of sins, followed by hunger and crop losses. Leviticus similarly announces discipline for sins followed by ineffective labor and land and trees failing to yield.
triples.source_text: And I will begin to strike you; I will obliterate you because of your sins.

target_units.text: And if up to this point you do not obey Me, I will discipline you seven times more for your sins.
And I will shatter the arrogance of your pride, and make your heaven iron, and your land as bronze;
and your strength shall be in vain. Your land shall not yield its seed, and the tree of your field shall not yield its fruit.

triples.relationship: shared curse of eating without satisfaction
triples.rationale: Micah says the people will eat but not be filled. Leviticus uses the same eating-without-being-filled warning within the covenant's scarcity-of-bread sanctions.
triples.source_text: You will eat but certainly not be filled. It will grow dark within you and turn aside, and you will certainly not be saved; whoever is saved will be handed over to the sword.

target_units.text: When I afflict you with a scarcity of bread, ten women shall bake your bread in one oven and give back your bread by weight. You shall eat and in no wise be filled.

triples.relationship: parallel loss of grain, wine and olive yield
triples.rationale: Micah announces sowing without reaping, pressing olives without anointing and pressing wine without drinking. Deuteronomy likewise warns of failed grain yield, vineyards whose wine is not drunk and olives that give no oil for anointing.
triples.source_text: You will sow but certainly not reap; you will press olives but certainly not anoint yourself with oil, and you will press wine, but you shall certainly not drink it. The ordinances of My people will be obliterated.

target_units.text: You shall carry much seed into the field, and gather little; for the locust shall devour it.
You shall plant a vineyard and dress it, but shall neither drink wine nor rejoice in it; for the worm shall devour it.
You shall have olive trees throughout all your borders, but shall not anoint yourself with oil; for your olives shall fall away.

triples.relationship: shared imagery of an absent fruit crop
triples.rationale: Micah laments the lack of an available cluster at the vintage. Jeremiah likewise describes vines without grapes and fig trees without figs. Both portray fruitlessness in passages that also address the people's wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: Alas! I have become like someone gathering stubble at harvest and a gleaning at vintage, with no cluster available to eat the first fruits. Alas, my soul,

target_units.text: and they will gather their produce, says the Lord. There is no grape on the vines and no figs on the fig trees, and the leaves have fallen.

triples.relationship: shared lament for vanished faithfulness
triples.rationale: Micah laments that the devout person has perished and no one acts rightly among people. The psalm similarly cries that the holy one is gone and truths have diminished, followed by deceit toward neighbors.
triples.source_text: for the devout person has perished from the earth, and no one acts rightly among people. They all litigate for bloodshed; each crushes his neighbor with crushing.

target_units.text: Save me, Lord, for the holy one is gone; for truths have become few among the sons of men.
Each spoke empty things to his neighbor; deceitful lips spoke with a heart and a heart.

triples.relationship: shared moth-consumption imagery of loss
triples.rationale: Micah pictures removal of the people's good things with a moth eating away. Isaiah likewise speaks of wool eaten by a moth, in contrast to God's lasting righteousness and salvation. The connection is the consuming-moth image; Micah's other wording remains unchanged.
triples.source_text: their good things like a moth eating away and walking upon a measuring rod on the day of watching. Woe, woe! Your punishments have arrived; now they will weep.

target_units.text: Listen to Me, you who know judgment, My people with My law in your heart. Do not fear people’s reproach or be overcome by their contempt.
For a garment will be consumed by time, and wool eaten by a moth. But My righteousness will last for ever, and My salvation through generations of generations.”

triples.relationship: parallel warning against trust in familiar companions
triples.rationale: Micah warns against confidence in friends and even disclosure to a bed companion. Jeremiah likewise warns people to guard against neighbors and not trust brothers because friends act deceitfully.
triples.source_text: Do not put confidence in friends or hope in leaders. With your bed companion, beware of entrusting anything to her.

target_units.text: Each of you, guard against his neighbor, and do not put trust in their brothers, because every brother will trip with the heel, and every friend will walk deceitfully.
Each will mock his friend; they certainly will not speak truth. Their tongue has learned to speak false things; they did wrong and did not cease turning back.

triples.relationship: explicitly corresponding household-division language
triples.rationale: Micah lists son against father, daughter against mother, daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and enemies within the household. Matthew reproduces the same family divisions and household-enemy statement in Jesus' description of division associated with His coming.
triples.source_text: For a son dishonors his father, a daughter will rise against her mother, a daughter-in-law will rise against her mother-in-law; a man’s enemies are all the men in his house.

target_units.text: For I came to divide a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law,
and a person’s enemies will be the members of his own household.

triples.relationship: waiting for the Lord and being heard
triples.rationale: Micah resolves to wait upon God the Savior and expects Him to listen. The psalm recalls waiting patiently for the Lord and being heard, giving an answered-prayer counterpart to that expectation.
triples.source_text: But I will look toward the Lord; I will wait upon God my Savior. My God will listen to me.

target_units.text: I waited patiently for the Lord; He attended to me and heard my supplication.

triples.relationship: falling, rising and forbidden enemy rejoicing
triples.rationale: Micah tells the enemy not to rejoice at his fall because he will rise. Proverbs likewise says the righteous fall and rise and then forbids rejoicing over an enemy's fall.
triples.source_text: Do not rejoice over me, my enemy, because I have fallen! I will rise, for if I sit in darkness, the Lord will shine for me.

target_units.text: for the righteous will fall seven times and rise, but the impious will grow weak amid evils.
If your enemy falls, do not rejoice over him, and at his tripping do not lift yourself up,
for the Lord will see, and it will not please Him, and He will turn His wrath away from him.

triples.relationship: acknowledgment of sin amid divine displeasure
triples.rationale: Micah accepts the Lord's anger because he has sinned, while awaiting vindication. Lamentations similarly questions grumbling over one's sin, calls for return to the Lord and acknowledges godlessness and unappeased divine displeasure.
triples.source_text: I will bear the Lord’s anger, for I sinned against Him, until He vindicates my case. He will execute my judgment and bring me out into the light; I will see His righteousness.

target_units.text: Why should a living person grumble, a man concerning his sin?
Our way was searched and examined; let us return to the Lord.
Let us lift our hearts upon our hands to the Exalted One in heaven.
We have sinned and acted godlessly, and Thou wast not propitiated.

triples.relationship: shared taunt about God's whereabouts
triples.rationale: Micah's enemy asks where the Lord his God is. The psalmist likewise hears the repeated taunt, Where is your God, while suffering in tears. Both place that question in the mouth of those aggravating the afflicted person's distress.
triples.source_text: My enemy will see and clothe herself in shame, she who says to me, “Where is the Lord your God?” My eyes will look upon her; now she will become a trampling place like mud in the streets

target_units.text: My tears became my bread day and night, while it is said to me every day, “Where is your God?”

triples.relationship: judgment according to the fruits of conduct
triples.rationale: Micah attributes the land's obliteration to the fruits of its inhabitants' practices. Jeremiah states that the Lord gives to each according to their ways and the fruits of their practices, articulating the principle behind such recompense.
triples.source_text: The land will become an obliteration together with those inhabiting it, from the fruits of their practices.

target_units.text: I, the Lord, examine hearts and test kidneys, to give each according to his ways and the fruits of his practices.

triples.relationship: prayer to Israel's divine shepherd
triples.rationale: Micah asks God to shepherd the people, described as the sheep of His inheritance. The psalm likewise addresses the One shepherding Israel and guiding Joseph like sheep, then asks Him to come and save.
triples.source_text: Shepherd Thy people with Thy rod, the sheep of Thine inheritance, camping by themselves in a forest amid Carmel. They will graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old.

target_units.text: Thou who shepherdest Israel, pay attention, Thou who guidest Joseph like sheep; Thou who sittest upon the cherubim, appear.
Before Ephraim and Benjamin and Manasseh, rouse Thy dominion, and come to save us.
God, turn us back; make Thy face shine, and we shall be saved.

triples.relationship: explicit recollection of the exodus as a pattern of wonders
triples.rationale: Micah promises wonders like those seen at the departure from Egypt. Exodus narrates the Lord rescuing Israel from the Egyptians and Israel seeing His great hand, providing the recalled deliverance pattern.
triples.source_text: And as in the days of your departure from Egypt, you will see wonderful things.

target_units.text: The Lord rescued Israel that day from the Egyptians’ hand, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead on the seashore.
Israel saw the great hand in what the Lord had done to the Egyptians. The people feared the Lord and trusted God and His attendant Moses.

triples.relationship: nations seeing and mouths falling silent
triples.rationale: Micah depicts nations seeing God's work and putting hands over their mouths. Isaiah likewise depicts nations marveling and kings closing their mouths as they see what had not been proclaimed to them. Both portray a silenced response to what they witness, in differing prophetic settings.
triples.source_text: Nations will see and be ashamed of all their strength. They will place hands over their mouth; their ears will be deafened.

target_units.text: so many nations will marvel at him, and kings will close their mouths. For those to whom he was not proclaimed will see, and those who have not heard will understand.

triples.relationship: shared serpent-and-earth humiliation imagery
triples.rationale: Micah compares the nations licking dust with snakes moving along the ground. Genesis condemns the serpent to go on breast and belly and eat earth. The connection is the degrading serpent-and-earth image, not an identification of the nations with that individual serpent.
triples.source_text: They will lick dust like snakes dragging along the earth; they will be thrown into turmoil in their confinement. They will be astonished at the Lord our God and fear Thee.

target_units.text: And the Lord God said to the serpent: Because you have done this, cursed are you above all cattle and all the wild beasts of the earth. Upon your breast and belly you shall go, and earth you shall eat all the days of your life.

triples.relationship: shared dust-licking image of humbled opponents
triples.rationale: Micah depicts the nations licking dust and fearing God. The royal psalm likewise describes enemies licking dust, with kings bowing and nations serving, using the same action to express humbled opposition.
triples.source_text: They will lick dust like snakes dragging along the earth; they will be thrown into turmoil in their confinement. They will be astonished at the Lord our God and fear Thee.

target_units.text: Ethiopians will fall before him, and his enemies will lick dust.
kings of Tarshish and the islands will offer gifts; kings of the Arabians and Saba will bring gifts.
And all kings will bow before him; all nations will serve him.

triples.relationship: shared question of God's incomparability
triples.rationale: Micah asks who is a God like the Lord in the context of mercy and forgiveness. The exodus song similarly asks who is like the Lord among the gods, praising His wondrous works. The shared rhetorical question introduces praise with different immediate emphases.
triples.source_text: Who is a God like Thee, removing injustices and passing over impieties for the remaining ones of His inheritance? He did not retain His anger as a testimony, because He desires mercy.

target_units.text: Who is like Thee among the gods, O Lord? Who is like Thee, glorified among the holy ones, marvellous in glories, working wonders?

triples.relationship: shared mercy and removal of wrongdoing
triples.rationale: Micah praises God for removing injustices, passing over impieties and desiring mercy. Exodus's proclamation of His name likewise emphasizes mercy and the taking away of lawlessness, injustice and sins.
triples.source_text: Who is a God like Thee, removing injustices and passing over impieties for the remaining ones of His inheritance? He did not retain His anger as a testimony, because He desires mercy.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

triples.relationship: spatial imagery of sins removed from the people
triples.rationale: Micah pictures injustices sunk and sins thrown into the sea's depths. The psalm describes lawless deeds removed as far as east from west. Both use distance or depth to portray God's removal of the people's wrongdoing.
triples.source_text: He Himself will turn back and pity us; He will sink our injustices, and they will be thrown into the depths of the sea—all our sins.

target_units.text: As far as the east is distant from the west, He removed our lawless deeds from us.

triples.relationship: appeal to the oath given to Abraham
triples.rationale: Micah asks for mercy to Abraham according to what God swore to the fathers. Genesis records the Lord swearing by Himself to bless Abraham's offspring and, through that offspring, the nations.
triples.source_text: Thou wilt grant truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, just as Thou didst swear to our fathers in the former days.

target_units.text: saying, “By Myself I have sworn, says the Lord: because you have done this thing, and have not spared your beloved son for My sake,
surely I will bless you, and greatly multiply your seed as the stars of the heaven, and as the sand upon the shore of the sea; and your seed shall inherit the cities of their adversaries.
And in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed, because you have listened to My voice.”

triples.relationship: shared appeal to ancestral mercy and Abraham's oath
triples.rationale: Micah joins mercy to Abraham with the oath sworn to the fathers. Luke's song likewise joins mercy to the fathers, remembrance of the holy covenant and the oath sworn to Abraham.
triples.source_text: Thou wilt grant truth to Jacob, mercy to Abraham, just as Thou didst swear to our fathers in the former days.

target_units.text: to show mercy to our fathers and remember His holy covenant,
the oath He swore to Abraham our father, to grant us
